\section*{I. Introduction}

\subsection*{AIR RAFT system identification, the art and science}

AIR RAFT system identification, the art and science \[ 1 \] of determining mathematical models of aircraft from flight test datasets, has become increasingly important in the development of new aircraft \[ 2 \]. As the field evolves \[ 3-7 \] the problems that can be solved at the state-of-the-art are often limited by what estimation methods can be run at the computational hardware available.

Maximum likelihood (ML) approaches such as the equation-error, output-error, and filter-error methods are widely used in aircraft system identification due to their assymptotic efficiency properties. When both process noise and measurement noise are considered, the ML estimator is the filter-error method (FEM), which employs a Kalman filter to approximate the prior predictive distribution of each measurement, given the previous measurements up to that point. There are multiple formulations of this method, but they either require solution of a Riccati equation, the most common approach in the aircraft literature \[ 8-10 \], Chap. 5\; or they require the estimation of the filter gain as an independent parameter \[ 11 \], the most common approach for black-box estimation, which can lead to unstable predictors in the optimization process. A consequence of these limitations is that the FEM requires good initial parameter estimates for convergence to occur.

Recently \[ 12,13 \], a new formulation of the ML estimator has been proposed for systems subject to process and measurement noise, using variational inference (VI). This approach was then reframed as unconstrained optimization and reparameterized for steady-state problems by the author in Ref. \[ 14 \], reducing the number of decision variables and complexity of the estimator. VI uses a different paradigm than the FEM for performing ML. The FEM uses a filter to approximate the prior predictive distribution and, assuming that distribution is correct, computes the likelihood. In VI, the estimation problem is augmented with the smoothing posterior distribution of the states, and a lower bound on the likelihood function is optimized instead. The approximation error between the candidate posterior and the true one is encoded in the objective function.

In this paper, the application of variational system identification is demonstrated for estimating aircraft parameters from flight-test data, an important use case of practical interest \[ 2 \]. This is also the first application of the method in non-simulated data. Our goal is to show that the estimator’s usefulness and its results as a drop-in replacement for the FEM and OEM. The results show that it is as good as, if not better than, those methods. In particular, convergence is attained with null initial guesses for all system parameters, in all examples tested in this paper.

### Page 3

对象的对称或反对称特性。### II. Problem Formulation
The goal of ML estimators for continuous-time dynamical systems is to obtain the vector $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n_0}$ of unknown parameters of a system modeled by the stochastic differential equation (SDE)
$$
d x(t) = f(x(t), u(t), \theta) \, dt + G(\theta) \, dW(t),
\tag{1}
$$
where $x : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$ are the states of the system, $u : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{n_u}$ are the known external inputs, and the model functions $f$ and $G$ are given. The SDE formulation is a more formal mathematical representation of the differential equation
$$
\dot{x}(t) = f(x(t), u(t), \theta) + G(\theta) w(t),
\tag{2}
$$
where $w(t)$ is the weak derivative of the Wiener process $W(t)$, i.e., white Gaussian noise with spectral density
$$
\mathbb{E} [w(t) w(\tau)^T] = \mathbb{I} \delta(t - \tau).
\tag{3}
$$
We consider a continuous-discrete formulation where the states are indirectly measured at discrete time instants through the output vector
$$
y_k = h(x(kT), u(kT), \theta) + v_k, \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, N;
\tag{4}
$$
where $k$ is the sample index, $v_k$ is the measurement noise, $T$ is the sampling period, and the output function $h$ is given. The measurement noise is assumed to be a zero-mean, white, Gaussian noise process, independent from the process noise, with constant covariance $R(\theta)$:
$$
\mathbb{E} \left[ v_i v_j^T \right] = R(\theta) \delta_{ij}, \qquad i, j = 0, 1, \ldots, N.
\tag{5}
$$
To apply the estimator, the SDE is discretized using a method such as the Euler-Maruyama scheme, chosen here for its simplicity. Given a prior distribution for the initial state $x_0$, the joint density of the discretized state path $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_N$, written in shorthand as $x_0 : N$, is
$$
p_\theta (x_0:N) = p_\theta (x_0) \prod_{k = 1}^N p_\theta(x_k | x_{k-1}),
\tag{6}
$$
where $p_\theta (x_0)$ is the initial-state prior density, and the state transition density under the Euler-Maruyama scheme is the multivariate normal with the following parameters:
$$
p_\theta (x_k | x_{k-1}) = \mathcal{N}(x_k; F(x_{k-1}, u_{k-1}, \theta), Q(\theta)),
\tag{7}
$$
$$
F(x_{k-1}, u_{k-1}, \theta) = x_k + T f(x_{k-1}, u_{k-1}, \theta),
\tag{8}
$$
$$
Q(\theta) = T G(\theta) G(\theta)^T.
\tag{9}
$$
Similarly, Eqs. (4)–(5) imply that
$$
p_\theta (y_k | x_k) = \mathcal{N}(y_k; h(x_k-1, u_k-1, \theta), R(\theta)),
\tag{10}
$$
$$
p_\theta (y_0:N | x_0:N) = \prod_{k=0}^N p_\theta(y_k | x_k),
\tag{11}
$$
laying the groundwork for applying the estimator.

### III. Variational Inference
In this section, the variational inference formulation of the maximum likelihood problem is derived, in a manner similar to [12, 14]. Starting from Bayes' rule,
$$
p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N) = \frac{p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N)}{p_\theta(y_0:N)},
\tag{12}
$$

### Page 4

discriminator.We have that for every $x_0:N$ in the support of the posterior, the likelihood $p_\theta(x_0:N)$ of a parameter vector $\theta$ is the ratio between the density of the complete data and the posterior:
$$p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N) = \frac{p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N)}{p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N)}. $$  (13)
This equation is not of practical use at any single state path $x_0:N$, but can be used to bound the likelihood when evaluated at a population of paths. For any density $q(x_0:N)$ whose support lies in the support of the posterior*, we have that
$$ log \, p_\theta(x_0:N) = log \left( \frac{p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N)}{q(x_0:N)} \times \frac{q(x_0:N)}{p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N)} \right) = log \left( \frac{p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N)}{q(x_0:N)} \right) + log \left( \frac{q(x_0:N)}{p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N)} \right).$$  (14)
Taking the expectation with respect to $q$, we have that
$$log \, p_\theta(x_0:N) = \int log \left( \frac{p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N)}{q(x_0:N)} \right) q(x_0:N) dx_0:N + \int log \left( \frac{q(x_0:N)}{p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N)} \right) q(x_0:N) dx_0:N.$$  (15)
The last term on the right-hand side of Eq. (15) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) of $q$ from the posterior, which is always non-negative
$$KLD[q(x_0:N) || p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N)] = \int log \left( \frac{q(x_0:N)}{p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N)} \right) q(x_0:N) dx_0:N \geq 0.$$  (16)
The KLD, also known as relative entropy, quantifies the difference between two probability distributions, being zero if and only if they are equal almost everywhere. This means that the first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (15) is a lower bound on the likelihood, or model evidence, which we will denote the evidence lower bound (ELBO),
$$L(\theta, q) := \int log \left( \frac{p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N)}{q(x_0:N)} \right) q(x_0:N) dx_0:N.$$  (17)
Substituting Eqs. (16)–(17) into Eq. (15), it is evident that the bound gets tighter as $q$ approaches the posterior, as quantified by the KLD:
$$log \, p_\theta(x_0:N) = L(\theta, q) + KLD[ q(x_0:N) || p_\theta(x_0:N | y_0:N) ] \geq L(\theta, q).$$  (18)
This lays out the basis of variational inference for maximum likelihood estimation: by searching for both the parameter vector $\theta$ and the density $q$ which maximize the ELBO $L(\theta, q)$, we are simultaneously maximizing the likelihood function and minimizing the divergence from $q$ to the true posterior. The density $q$, called the assumed density, should be chosen from a family of distributions $Q$ that is general enough to yield tight bounds, but still be tractable enough to compute and optimize the ELBO. The ML estimation problem using VI is then
$$maximize_{q \in Q, \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n} L(\theta, q).$$  (19)
In situations where the true posterior is contained in $Q$, this formulation is equivalent to ML estimation. When the likelihood function is intractable to compute, as it is in parameter estimation of nonlinear systems, VI with its assured lower bound offers stronger theoretical guarantees than when approximations like the extended Kalman filter or particle smoothers are used to compute and maximize the likelihood [15, 16].
VI can also be understood as a regularized generalization of maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation over a population of points [see 14, Sec. 3.2]. Eq. (17) can be split into the expected complete-data log-density and the differential entropy of the assumed density $q$:
$$L(\theta, q) = \int log \, p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N) q(x_0:N) dx_0:N - \int log \, q(x_0:N) q(x_0:N) dx_0:N.$$  (20)
$$= \int log \, p_\theta(x_0:N, y_0:N) q(x_0:N) dx_0:N + h_q[X_0:N].$$  (21)
In MAP estimation, a single state path is chosen as the most probable, given the observations. In VI, a population of paths, defined by $q$, is chosen to take into account the uncertainty in the states. The differential entropy of the population of paths $h_q[X_0:N]$, which increases as the population is spread out over a larger region, is included to prevent the population from collapsing at a single point, the posterior mode.

Instead of having an expectation over a high-dimensional space, this form of the ELBO only requires expectation over the states at each time sample or at consecutive time-sample pairs. This allows integration using sigma points, which is exact for linear systems and a reasonable approximation for nonlinear systems under small deviations from trim.

For simplicity, in this paper we use sigma points without the center one, which gives all remaining points equal weight. If we let \( x^{(i)}_k \) denote the sigma points associated with \( q(x_k) \) or \( q(x_{k-1:k}) \), the objective function is then

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta, q) = \frac{1}{2n_x} \sum_{i=1}^{2n_x} p_{\theta}(x^{(i)}_0) + \frac{1}{4n_x} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \sum_{i=1}^{4n_x} \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)}_k|x^{(i)}_{k-1}) + \frac{1}{2n_x} \sum_{k=0}^{N} \sum_{i=1}^{2n_x} \log p_{\theta}(y_k|x^{(i)}_k) + \frac{1}{2} \log \det \Sigma_{\text{marg}} + \frac{N}{2} \log \det \Sigma_{\text{cond}} + \text{const}. \quad (27)\]

This function can then be maximized using standard nonlinear programming packages. Note that \( x^{(i)}_k \) depend on \( q \) and its underlying parameters. Changes in \( \mu_{0:N} \) translate all sigma points by some amount, while increasing \( \Sigma_{\text{marg}} \) increases their spread, decreasing the average log-density but increasing the entropy. The optimum balances these competing criteria.
